entries.text: In 1972, a small spacecraft set out for the outer planets.
Its destination was Jupiter. No one had explored that world up close.
In less than 11 hours, it had crossed the Moon’s orbit.
Spinning helped keep the spacecraft stable during its journey.
Far from the Sun, its generators turned radioactive heat into electricity.
Between Mars and Jupiter, the asteroid belt held an unanswered question.
Would there be enough particles to damage the spacecraft?
Imagine the fear of finding a path crowded with rocks...
But the real crossing was not a maze. The asteroids were very far apart.
The instruments searched for something smaller: dust particles.
After months of measurements, Pioneer emerged from the belt undamaged.
By late 1973, Jupiter began to fill the frame.
Each message took tens of minutes. The team had to plan ahead.
To see this world, an image would have to emerge a little at a time.
Pioneer did not have a camera like the one in a phone.
Its spin scanned the planet. Narrow strips built the image.
The instrument measured red and blue light.
Jupiter’s radiation triggered unwanted commands in the instrument.
The team sent recovery sequences. The observations continued.
On Earth, processing also estimated green and assembled the image.
Some images were lost, including Io’s. But so much reached us.
This is Ganymede, seen by Pioneer 10 in 1973.
Light, radiation and magnetism: a new world to study.
The spacecraft carried something else: an introduction to its makers.
Hydrogen: a reference for measuring time and size.
Pulsars: stars that help locate our Sun.
The third planet is where the journey began: Earth.
Pioneer itself provides a scale for the human figures.
People: one raises a hand, as if to say hello.
A gold-colored aluminum plaque. A message for a meeting that may never happen.
The journey did not end at Jupiter. Its gravity changed Pioneer’s path.
By 1983, it was traveling beyond the planets’ orbits.
As years passed, the generators supplied less power. The team had to choose what stayed on.
In 1998, Voyager 1 became the farthest from the Sun, traveling in another direction.
Pioneer had shown the way. Now Earth was listening farther and farther away.
The distance grew. Earth’s antennas searched for an ever weaker signal.
March 2002. Thirty years after launch, it was still responding.
April 2002. The last data from its instruments reached Earth.
January 2003. A last signal took 11 hours and 20 minutes to arrive.
February 2003. No signal detected.
Without enough power to reach us, Pioneer fell silent.
Silence did not stop the journey.
Pioneer continues in the direction of Aldebaran, a distant star.
We are talking about millions of years. A future none of us here will see.
Those who go first open a path for many.
